bib.title: Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents", Yilin Xiao, Zhehan Zhu, Yujing Zhang, Jin Chen, Zijin Hong, Luyao Zhuang, Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Xiaocao Ouyang, Lingfei Ren, Xiao Huang. arXiv:2607.29377v1 [cs.CL], 31 Jul 2026. It is a preprint with no venue named. The authors say code will follow "after peer review". The format looks like an AAAI-style submission, but the paper doesn't say so.

COVERAGE: All 43,078 of 43,078 chars read, including the tables, figure text and references. The paper has no limitations section and no appendix in the extraction. The text says "Additional baseline descriptions are provided in the Appendix", but that appendix is not in the PDF I was given.

FIT WARNING: This is a partial fit. The paper is about retrieval-time memory for conversational and QA agents. It is not about learning from experience, such as trajectories, skills or reflection. For "raw vs distilled" it is a clean data point for raw storage, and its efficiency table gives cost numbers. It has no no-memory baseline, and its "full-context" baseline is a sliding-window variant. Reflexion (Shinn 2023) and Voyager (Wang 2024) appear only as citations, not as baselines.

CLAIMS
1. Raw traces plus structured retrieval, with no LLM calls in the memory pipeline, beat every LLM-generated-memory baseline on LoCoMo.
   - number: average F1 59.15 vs GAM 53.75 (GPT-4o-mini). The text reports gaps of 5.40 and 5.45 points on average F1 and BLEU-1.
   - setup: LoCoMo, four question types, GPT-4o-mini reader, top-5 retrieval cap for every method. Only the final-QA reader calls an LLM.
   - quote: "Relative to GAM, the strongest overall baseline, it improves average F1 and BLEU-1 by 5.40 and 5.45 points with GPT-4o-mini, and by 4.87 and 4.86 points with Qwen2.5-14B, respectively."
   - where: Main Results, Table 1

2. Distilled-memory systems often score below the memory-free baselines.
   - number: with GPT-4o-mini, A-Mem 39.65, LightMem 38.44 and MemoryOS 42.84 average F1, against RAG 44.73 and LONG-LLM 37.31. Mem0 scores 45.10.
   - setup: LoCoMo, GPT-4o-mini. With Qwen2.5-14B, A-Mem 28.98, Mem0 36.04 and LightMem 31.39 all fall below RAG 38.27 and LONG-LLM 38.31.
   - quote: "RAG 52.45 47.94 27.50 20.13 46.07 40.35 23.23 17.94 44.73 39.40" and "A-Mem 33.75 30.04 22.09 15.28 27.19 22.05 13.49 10.74 28.98 24.47"
   - where: Table 1

3. Memory-operation cost: zero LLM tokens, lower latency, higher accuracy.
   - number: baselines use 14.1M (SimpleMem), 0.88M (LightMem) and 28.6M (GAM) memory-operation tokens. Zero-Mem uses 0. Time is 334.77 s total (0.22 s per query), against 788.76 s for LightMem, the fastest baseline, which is the 57.6% reduction.
   - setup: LoCoMo, GPT-4o-mini, four concurrent threads, identical hardware. Only SimpleMem, LightMem and GAM were compared. Tokens exclude the shared final-QA stage and encoder compute.
   - quote: "SimpleMem 48.02 41.68 14,096,246 9,153.41 8,365.38 5.43 ... GAM 53.75 47.51 28,570,674 18,552.39 9,237.25 6.00 Zero-Mem (Ours) 59.15 52.96 0 0 334.77 0.22"
   - where: Table 2 and Efficiency Comparison

4. Zero-token is not zero compute.
   - number: none
   - setup: the encoder (BGE-M3), NER (spaCy), BM25, PageRank and calibration still run.
   - quote: "Zero-token operation does not imply zero computation, since encoder inference, memory organization, retrieval, and deterministic calibration still incur processing costs."
   - where: Efficiency Comparison

5. On long-context HotpotQA, Zero-Mem leads at every length. Most generative-memory systems degrade badly there and trail the memory-free baselines.
   - number: at 56K with GPT-4o-mini, Zero-Mem 72.07 F1, GAM 63.22, RAG 52.71, LONG-LLM 56.56. Mem0 32.58 and A-Mem 33.90. At 448K with GPT-4o-mini, Zero-Mem 65.04 against RAG 54.01. The average gain over the strongest baseline is 5.52 points.
   - setup: HotpotQA in the MemAgent variant, with 56K, 224K and 448K-token contexts, F1.
   - quote: "Zero-Mem achieves the highest F1 across all readers and contexts lengths, including the challenging 448K-token setting, with an average improvement of 5.52 points over the strongest baseline." The extraction reads "across all readers and context lengths".
   - where: Table 3

6. Ablation: both views are needed, and the graph view matters more on multi-hop QA.
   - number: full model 72.07 F1; graph only 62.50; hierarchy only 54.88; without closure 67.90; without calibration 70.13.
   - setup: HotpotQA, 56K tokens, GPT-4o-mini.
   - quote: "Retaining only the graph view reduces the scores to 62.50 and 59.90, whereas retaining only the hierarchical view yields 54.88 and 51.40."
   - where: Ablation Study, Figure 3

7. Retrieval budget has diminishing returns.
   - number: average F1 goes from 52.59 at top-1 to 59.15 at top-5. Top-5 trails the best setting (top-10) by 0.65 F1.
   - setup: LoCoMo, GPT-4o-mini.
   - quote: "this configuration trails Top-10 by only 0.65 F1 and 0.83 BLEU-1 while retaining half as many primary candidates."
   - where: Figure 4

BASELINES AND TOKEN MATCHING
- Memory-free baselines:
  - LONG-LLM splits the history into sliding-window blocks, answers each block independently and returns the most confident answer.
  - RAG uses 2,048-token chunks and takes the top 5.
- Memory-based baselines: A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS, LightMem, SimpleMem, CompassMem, GAM, plus HippoRAG on LoCoMo.
- There is no no-memory (empty context) baseline.
- Matching is only partial. The paper says "all methods use an identical final-QA reader and equivalent context budget". Retrieved items are capped at five for every method. LONG-LLM's sliding window clearly does not follow that cap, and its token use is not reported. No per-method reader-token counts are given.
- Cost in Table 2 covers memory operations only, for three baselines, on LoCoMo only. Baseline scores appear to be reused from GAM and SimpleMem protocols ("We follow the evaluation metrics and protocols established in prior work").

LIMITS
- The authors state no limitations.
- Single-run numbers with no variance, seeds or significance tests.
- Only two benchmarks. Both are QA over static histories, with no agent actions, tool use, task success or memory updates and conflict resolution beyond retrieval.
- Table 2 times include the baselines' LLM API latency under four threads. Zero-Mem ran on local RTX 4090 GPUs. The comparison is not hardware-clean for API-bound methods, and the fastest baseline is the only one near parity.
- Query profiling uses deterministic rules and NER. Zero-Mem's strength on HotpotQA may be tied to entity-heavy Wikipedia text.
- Possible tuning: ρ and γ were both set to 0.6. The paper doesn't say how they were chosen. It also doesn't say whether top-k was tuned on test data. Figure 4 shows top-10 is better than the reported top-5.
- Code is not yet released.
- The GAM top-5 constraint may disadvantage deep-research-style baselines.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- GAM (Yan et al. 2025, arXiv:2511.18423): benchmark protocol and strongest baseline.
- SimpleMem (Liu et al. 2026, ICML) and LightMem (Fang et al. 2026, ICLR): efficiency baselines.
- HippoRAG (Gutierrez et al. 2024, NeurIPS): graph and Personalized PageRank idea.
- Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025), A-Mem (Xu et al. 2025, NeurIPS), MemoryOS (Kang et al. 2025, EMNLP), CompassMem (Hu et al. 2026a), Zep (Rasmussen et al. 2025).
- LoCoMo (Maharana et al. 2024, ACL); HotpotQA (Yang et al. 2018); MemAgent (Yu et al. 2026, ICLR) for the HotpotQA variant.
- Context: Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), Voyager (Wang et al. 2024), MemoryBank (Zhong et al. 2024), Xu, Szlam and Weston 2022.

CODE: none, and no pseudocode. The equations are the Personalized PageRank update (Eq. 10) and the score fusion S_fuse = ρ·S_primary + (1−ρ)·S_secondary (Eq. 13).

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (page 1): compares three memory regimes: generative memory, raw retrieval, and Zero-Mem. It is the quickest way to show raw versus distilled memory.
- Figure 3 (the ablation, referenced above) is a second option if wanted.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. The extraction has missing spaces in places, and table and figure text is flattened. I checked the numbers by hand: Table 2's 57.6% matches total time (788.76 to 334.77). The per-query times (0.51 to 0.22) give about 57%, which is rounding.
